title: Book 3, Chapter 10 — Fifth Year of the War—Trial and Execution of the Plataeans— Corcyraean Revolution
paragraphs: In the same summer, after Lesbos had been reduced, the Athenians under Nicias, son of Niceratus, made an expedition against the island of Minoa. It lies off Megara, and the Megarians used it as a fortified post, having built a tower on it. Nicias wanted the Athenians to keep up their blockade from this nearer station instead of from Budorum and Salamis. He meant to stop the Peloponnesian galleys and privateers from slipping out of the island unobserved, as they had been in the habit of doing, and at the same time to keep anything from coming into Megara. So he first took two towers projecting on the side of Nisaea, by engines from the sea, and cleared the entrance to the channel between the island and the shore. He then cut off all communication by building a wall on the mainland, at the point where a bridge over a morass allowed reinforcements to be thrown into the island, which was not far from the continent. A few days were enough to finish this. After that he raised some works on the island itself, left a garrison there, and withdrew with his forces.

At about the same time in this summer, the Plataeans, who had run out of provisions and could no longer hold out against the siege, surrendered to the Peloponnesians. It happened in this way. An assault had been made on the wall, and the Plataeans were unable to repel it. The Lacedaemonian commander saw how weak they were and wished to avoid taking the place by storm. His instructions from Lacedaemon had been drawn up with this in view: if peace were ever made with Athens, and each side agreed to give back the places it had taken in the war, Plataea would then be held to have come over voluntarily and would not be included in the list. So he sent a herald to ask whether they were willing to surrender the town voluntarily to the Lacedaemonians and accept them as their judges, on the understanding that the guilty would be punished but no one without due process of law. The Plataeans were now at the last point of weakness, and as soon as the herald had delivered his message they surrendered the town. The Peloponnesians fed them for some days, until the judges from Lacedaemon arrived. There were five of them. When they came, no charge was brought. They simply called the Plataeans up and asked whether they had done the Lacedaemonians and their allies any service in the war then raging. The Plataeans asked leave to speak at greater length and appointed two of their number to represent them: Astymachus, son of Asopolaus, and Lacon, son of Aeimnestus, proxenus of the Lacedaemonians. These came forward and spoke as follows:

“Lacedaemonians, when we surrendered our city we trusted in you. We expected a trial more in keeping with the forms of law than this one, which we never imagined we should face. We also consented to place ourselves in the hands of you and you only, from whom we thought we were most likely to obtain justice, and not of other judges, as is now the case. As matters stand, we are afraid that we have been deceived twice over. We have good reason to suspect not only that the issue to be tried is the most terrible of all, but also that you will not prove impartial. We argue this from the fact that no accusation was first brought forward for us to answer, but we ourselves had to ask leave to speak, and from the fact that the question was put so briefly that a true answer to it tells against us, while a false one can be contradicted. In this dilemma our safest course, and indeed our only one, seems to be to say something whatever the risk. In our position we could hardly stay silent without being tormented by the damning thought that speaking might have saved us. We face another difficulty as well, that of convincing you. If we were strangers to each other, we might gain by bringing forward new matter that you did not know. As it is, we can tell you nothing that you do not know already. And what we fear is not that you have judged us in your own minds to have failed in our duty toward you and make this our crime, but that, to please a third party, we are submitting to a trial whose result has already been decided. Nevertheless, we will lay before you what we can justly urge, not only on the question of the quarrel that the Thebans have against us, but also as addressing you and the rest of the Hellenes. We will remind you of our good services and endeavor to prevail with you.

“You ask us briefly whether we have done the Lacedaemonians and their allies any service in this war. If you ask us as enemies, we say that to refrain from serving you was not to do you injury. If you ask us as friends, we say that you are the more at fault for having marched against us. During the peace, and against the Mede, we acted well. We have not now been the first to break the peace, and we were the only Boeotians who then joined in defending the liberty of Hellas against the Mede. Although we are an inland people, we were present at the action at Artemisium. In the battle fought in our territory we fought at the side of you and Pausanias. And in all the other Hellenic exploits of that time we took a part quite out of proportion to our strength. Besides, you as Lacedaemonians ought not to forget that when a great panic seized Sparta after the earthquake, caused by the secession of the Helots to Ithome, we sent a third of our citizens to assist you.

“On these great and memorable occasions such was the part we chose, although afterward we became your enemies. For this you were to blame. When we asked for your alliance against our Theban oppressors, you rejected our petition and told us to go to the Athenians, who were our neighbors, since you lived too far off. In the war we never did you, and never would have done you, anything unreasonable. If we refused to desert the Athenians when you asked us, we did no wrong. They had helped us against the Thebans when you drew back, and we could no longer give them up with honor. This was all the more so because we had obtained their alliance and had been admitted to their citizenship at our own request, after receiving benefits at their hands. It was plainly our duty to obey their orders loyally. Besides, the faults that either of you may commit in your supremacy must be laid not on the followers but on the chiefs who lead them astray.

“As for the Thebans, they have wronged us repeatedly, and you yourselves know their last aggression, which has brought us to our present position. They seized our city in time of peace, and what is more, at a holy time of the month. They justly met our vengeance, in accordance with the universal law that sanctions resistance to an invader, and it cannot now be right that we should suffer on their account. If you take your own immediate interest and their animosity as the test of justice, you will prove yourselves to be waiters on expediency rather than judges of right. Yet if they seem useful to you now, we and the rest of the Hellenes gave you much more valuable help at a time of greater need. Now you are the assailants, and others fear you. But at the crisis we speak of, when the barbarian threatened everyone with slavery, the Thebans were on his side. It is just, therefore, to set our patriotism then against our error now, if error there has been. You will find that the merit outweighs the fault. It was shown at a time when few Hellenes would set their valor against the strength of Xerxes, and when greater praise went to those who preferred the dangerous path of honor to the safe course of consulting their own interest in face of the invasion. We were among those few, and highly were we honored for it. And yet we now fear to perish for having acted on the same principles again, and for having chosen to act well with Athens rather than wisely with Sparta. Yet in justice the same cases should be decided in the same way. Policy should mean nothing else than lasting gratitude for the service of a good ally, combined with proper attention to one’s own immediate interest.

“Consider also that the Hellenes generally now regard you as a pattern of worth and honor. This is no obscure cause. You, the judges, are as illustrious as we, the prisoners, are blameless. If you pass an unjust sentence on us, take care that men do not take offense at an unworthy decision in the matter of honorable men, made by men yet more honorable than they, and at spoils taken from the Plataeans, the benefactors of Hellas, being consecrated in the national temples. It will seem shocking indeed that Lacedaemonians should destroy Plataea, and that the city whose name your fathers inscribed on the tripod at Delphi for its good service should be blotted out by you from the map of Hellas to please the Thebans. To such a depth of misfortune have we fallen that, while the success of the Medes had been our ruin, the Thebans now supplant us in your once fond regard. We have been exposed to two dangers, the greatest of any: that of dying of starvation then, if we had not surrendered our town, and now that of being tried for our lives. So we Plataeans, after exertions beyond our power in the cause of the Hellenes, are rejected by all, forsaken and unassisted. None of our allies helps us, and we are reduced to doubting the stability of our only hope, yourselves.

“Still, in the name of the gods who once presided over our confederacy, and of our own good service in the Hellenic cause, we adjure you to relent. We ask you to recall the decision that we fear the Thebans may have obtained from you, and to ask back the gift you have given them, so that they do not disgrace you by slaying us. Gain a pure gratitude instead of a guilty one, and do not gratify others only to be rewarded yourselves with shame. Our lives may be quickly taken, but it will be a heavy task to wipe away the infamy of the deed. We are no enemies whom you might justly punish, but friends forced to take arms against you. To grant us our lives would therefore be a righteous judgment, if you also consider that we are prisoners who surrendered of their own accord, stretching out our hands for quarter, that Hellenic law forbids their slaughter, and that we were always your benefactors besides. Look at the tombs of your fathers, slain by the Medes and buried in our country. Year by year we honored them with garments and all other dues, and with the first-fruits of everything our land produced in its season, as friends from a friendly country and allies of their old companions in arms. If you do not decide aright, your conduct will be the very opposite of ours. Consider only this: Pausanias buried them thinking that he was laying them in friendly ground and among men as friendly. But you, if you kill us and make the Plataean territory Theban, will leave your fathers and kinsmen in hostile soil, among their murderers, deprived of the honors they now enjoy. What is more, you will enslave the land in which the freedom of the Hellenes was won, make desolate the temples of the gods to whom they prayed before they overcame the Medes, and take away your ancestral sacrifices from those who founded and instituted them.

“It would not be to your glory, Lacedaemonians, to offend in this way against the common law of the Hellenes and against your own ancestors, or to kill us, your benefactors, to gratify another’s hatred when you have not been wronged yourselves. It would be more glorious to spare us and to yield to the impulse of reasonable compassion. Reflect not merely on the awful fate in store for us, but also on the character of the sufferers, and on the impossibility of predicting how soon misfortune may fall even on those who do not deserve it. As we have a right to do, and as our need compels us, we entreat you, calling aloud on the gods at whose common altar all the Hellenes worship, to hear our request and not to be unmindful of the oaths that your fathers swore and that we now plead. We supplicate you by the tombs of your fathers, and appeal to those who are gone to save us from falling into the hands of the Thebans, and to keep their dearest friends from being given up to their most detested foes. We also remind you of that day on which we did the most glorious deeds at your fathers’ sides, we who on this day are likely to suffer the most dreadful fate. Finally, we come to what is necessary and yet most difficult for men in our situation, that is, to make an end of speaking, since with that ending the peril of our lives draws near. In conclusion we say that we did not surrender our city to the Thebans (we would have preferred inglorious starvation to that), but trusted in you and capitulated to you. If we fail to persuade you, it would be just to put us back in the same position and let us take whatever chance falls to us. And at the same time we adjure you not to give us up out of your hands and your good faith, Lacedaemonians, we your suppliants, we Plataeans, foremost of the Hellenic patriots, to the Thebans, our most hated enemies. Be our saviors instead, and do not, while you free the rest of the Hellenes, bring us to destruction.”

Such were the words of the Plataeans. The Thebans were afraid that the Lacedaemonians might be moved by what they had heard. They came forward and said that they too wished to address the judges, since the Plataeans had been allowed to speak at length, against their wishes, instead of being confined to a simple answer to the question. Leave was granted, and the Thebans spoke as follows:

“We should never have asked to make this speech if the Plataeans had contented themselves with answering the question briefly. Instead they turned around and made charges against us, together with a long defense of themselves on matters outside the present inquiry and not even the subject of accusation, and with praise of what no one finds fault with. However, since they have done so, we must answer their charges and refute their self-praise. Then neither our bad name nor their good one will help them, and you will hear the real truth on both points and decide accordingly.

“The origin of our quarrel was this. We settled Plataea some time after the rest of Boeotia, together with other places from which we had driven the mixed population. The Plataeans did not choose to recognize our supremacy, as had been first arranged, but separated themselves from the rest of the Boeotians and proved traitors to their nationality. We used compulsion, and they went over to the Athenians and did us as much harm with them, and we retaliated.

“Next, when the barbarian invaded Hellas, they say that they were the only Boeotians who did not Medize. This is what they most glorify themselves for, and where they most abuse us. We say that if they did not Medize, it was because the Athenians did not do so either. In the same way afterward, when the Athenians attacked the Hellenes, the Plataeans were again the only Boeotians who Atticized. And yet consider the forms of our respective governments when we so acted. At that time our city had neither an oligarchical constitution, in which all the nobles enjoy equal rights, nor a democracy. It had the form most opposed to law and good government and nearest to a tyranny, the rule of a close cabal. These men hoped to strengthen their individual power by the success of the Mede. They kept the people down by force and brought him into the town. The city as a whole was not its own mistress when it so acted, and ought not to be reproached for the errors it committed while deprived of its constitution. Examine only how we acted after the Mede had departed and we had recovered our constitution. The Athenians were then attacking the rest of Hellas and endeavoring to subjugate our country, most of which faction had already made them masters of. Did we not fight and conquer at Coronea and liberate Boeotia? And do we not now actively contribute to the liberation of the rest, providing horses for the cause and a force unequaled by that of any other state in the confederacy?

“Let this suffice to excuse us for our Medism. We will now endeavor to show that you have injured the Hellenes more than we have, and deserve condign punishment more. You say it was in defense against us that you became allies and citizens of Athens. If so, you ought only to have called in the Athenians against us, instead of joining them in attacking others. It was open to you to do this if you ever felt that they were leading you where you did not wish to follow. Lacedaemon was already your ally against the Mede, as you so much insist, and this was surely enough to keep us off, and above all to let you deliberate in security. Nevertheless, you chose of your own accord, without compulsion, to throw in your lot with Athens. And you say it would have been base to betray your benefactors. But it was surely far baser and more iniquitous to sacrifice the whole body of the Hellenes, your fellow confederates, who were liberating Hellas, than the Athenians only, who were enslaving it. The return you made them was therefore neither equal nor honorable. You called them in, as you say, because you were being oppressed yourselves, and then became their accomplices in oppressing others. Yet baseness lies rather in not returning like for like than in not returning what is justly due but must be unjustly paid.

“Meanwhile we have plainly shown that it was not for the sake of the Hellenes that you alone then did not Medize, but because the Athenians did not Medize either, and you wished to side with them and be against the rest. Yet you now claim the benefit of good deeds done to please your neighbors. This cannot be admitted. You chose the Athenians, and with them you must stand or fall. Nor can you plead the league then made and claim that it should now protect you. You abandoned that league, and offended against it by helping, instead of hindering, the subjugation of the Aeginetans and other members of it. You did so not under compulsion, but while enjoying the same institutions that you enjoy to the present hour, with no one forcing you as in our case. Lastly, before you were blockaded, an invitation was addressed to you to be neutral and join neither party. This you did not accept. Who then more justly merit the detestation of the Hellenes than you, who sought their ruin under the mask of honor? The former virtues that you allege you now show not to be proper to your character. The real bent of your nature has at length been damningly proved: when the Athenians took the path of injustice, you followed them.

“This, then, is our explanation of our unwilling Medism and your willful Atticizing. The last wrong of which you complain is that we lawlessly invaded your town in time of peace and festival, as you say. Here again we cannot think that we were more in fault than you. If of our own motion we made an armed attack on your city and ravaged your territory, we are guilty. But if the first men among you in estate and family wished to put an end to the foreign connection and to restore you to the common Boeotian country, and invited us of their own free will, where is our crime? Where wrong is done, those who lead, as you say, are more to blame than those who follow. Not that in our judgment wrong was done either by them or by us. They were citizens like yourselves, with more at stake than you. They opened their own walls and introduced us into their own city, not as foes but as friends. Their aim was to prevent the bad among you from becoming worse, to give honest men their due, and to reform principles without attacking persons. You were not to be banished from your city but brought home to your kindred, nor to be made enemies to any, but friends alike to all.

“That our intention was not hostile is proved by our behavior. We did no harm to anyone, but publicly invited those who wished to live under a national Boeotian government to come over to us. At first you gladly did so, made an agreement with us and remained tranquil, until you became aware of the smallness of our numbers. Now it is possible that there was something not quite fair in our entering without the consent of your commons. At any rate you did not repay us in kind. Instead of refraining from violence, as we had done, and inducing us to retire by negotiation, you fell on us in violation of your agreement. You slew some of us in the fighting, and of that we do not so much complain, for there was a certain justice in it. But others who held out their hands and received quarter, and whose lives you afterward promised us, you lawlessly butchered. If this was not abominable, what is? And after these three crimes committed one after the other, the violation of your agreement, the murder of the men afterward, and the lying breach of your promise not to kill them if we refrained from injuring your property in the country, you still affirm that we are the criminals and pretend that you yourselves will escape justice. Not so, if these your judges decide aright. You will be punished for all together.

“Such, Lacedaemonians, are the facts. We have gone into them at some length both on your account and on our own. We want you to feel that you will justly condemn the prisoners, and we want to feel that we have given an additional sanction to our vengeance. We would also prevent you from being melted by hearing of their past virtues, if they ever had any. These may fairly be appealed to by the victims of injustice, but they only aggravate the guilt of criminals, since criminals offend against their better nature. Nor let them gain anything by crying and wailing, by calling on your fathers’ tombs and on their own desolate condition. Against this we point to the far more dreadful fate of our youth, butchered at their hands. The fathers of these youths either fell at Coronea, bringing Boeotia over to you, or sit as forlorn old men by desolate hearths, and they have far more reason to implore your justice upon the prisoners. The pity that the Plataeans appeal to is rather due to men who suffer unworthily. Those who suffer justly, as they do, are on the contrary subjects for triumph. For their present desolate condition they have themselves to blame, since they willfully rejected the better alliance. Their lawless act was not provoked by any action of ours. Hate, not justice, inspired their decision. And even now the satisfaction they afford us is not adequate. They will suffer by a legal sentence, not, as they pretend, as suppliants asking for quarter in battle, but as prisoners who have surrendered on agreement to take their trial. Vindicate, therefore, Lacedaemonians, the Hellenic law that they have broken. And to us, the victims of its violation, grant the reward our zeal has merited. Do not let us be supplanted in your favor by their harangues. Offer an example to the Hellenes that the contests to which you invite them are of deeds, not words. Good deeds can be stated briefly, but where wrong is done a wealth of language is needed to veil its deformity. However, if leading powers were to do what you are now doing, and were to put one short question to all alike and decide accordingly, men would be less tempted to seek fine phrases to cover bad actions.”

Such were the words of the Thebans. The Lacedaemonian judges decided that the question whether they had received any service from the Plataeans in the war was a fair one for them to put. They had always invited the Plataeans to be neutral, in keeping with the original covenant of Pausanias after the defeat of the Mede, and had again offered them the same conditions definitely before the blockade. The Plataeans had refused this offer, and the judges conceived that, by the loyalty of their own intention, they were now released from the covenant. Having, as they considered, suffered evil at the hands of the Plataeans, they brought them in again one by one and asked each of them the same question, that is, whether they had done the Lacedaemonians and allies any service in the war. When a man said that he had not, they took him out and slew him, without exception. The Plataeans thus massacred numbered not less than two hundred, together with twenty-five Athenians who had shared in the siege. The women were taken as slaves. The Thebans gave the city for about a year to some political emigrants from Megara and to the surviving Plataeans of their own party to inhabit. Afterward they razed it to the ground from the very foundations. Next to the precinct of Hera they built an inn two hundred feet square, with rooms all around above and below, using for this purpose the roofs and doors of the Plataeans. Of the rest of the materials in the wall, the brass and the iron, they made couches, which they dedicated to Hera, and for her they also built a stone chapel a hundred feet square. The land they confiscated and let out on a ten years’ lease to Theban occupiers. The Lacedaemonians’ adverse attitude in the whole Plataean affair was adopted mainly to please the Thebans, who were thought to be useful in the war then raging. Such was the end of Plataea, in the ninety-third year after she became the ally of Athens.

Meanwhile the forty ships of the Peloponnesians that had gone to the relief of the Lesbians, and that we left fleeing across the open sea with the Athenians in pursuit, were caught in a storm off Crete. They scattered from there and made their way to Peloponnese. At Cyllene they found thirteen Leucadian and Ambraciot galleys, with Brasidas, son of Tellis, who had lately arrived as counsellor to Alcidas. The Lacedaemonians, now that the Lesbian expedition had failed, had resolved to strengthen their fleet and sail to Corcyra, where a revolution had broken out. They meant to arrive before the twelve Athenian ships at Naupactus could be reinforced from Athens. Brasidas and Alcidas began to prepare accordingly.

The Corcyraean revolution began with the return of the prisoners taken in the sea-fights off Epidamnus. The Corinthians had released them, nominally on the security of eight hundred talents given by their proxeni, but in reality on their engagement to bring Corcyra over to Corinth. These men set about canvassing each of the citizens and intriguing to detach the city from Athens. An Athenian and a Corinthian vessel arrived with envoys on board, and a conference was held, in which the Corcyraeans voted to remain allies of the Athenians according to their agreement, but to be friends of the Peloponnesians as they had been formerly. Meanwhile the returned prisoners brought to trial Peithias, a volunteer proxenus of the Athenians and leader of the commons, on the charge of enslaving Corcyra to Athens. He was acquitted, and in retaliation accused five of the richest of their number of cutting stakes in the ground sacred to Zeus and Alcinous, the legal penalty being a stater for each stake. They were convicted, and since the amount of the penalty was very large, they seated themselves as suppliants in the temples, to be allowed to pay it by installments. But Peithias, who was a member of the senate, prevailed on that body to enforce the law. The accused were rendered desperate by the law, and they also learned that Peithias intended, while still a member of the senate, to persuade the people to conclude a defensive and offensive alliance with Athens. They banded together, armed with daggers, burst suddenly into the senate, and killed Peithias and sixty others, senators and private persons. Only a few of the party of Peithias took refuge in the Athenian galley, which had not yet departed.

After this outrage, the conspirators called the Corcyraeans to an assembly. They said that this would turn out for the best and would save them from being enslaved by Athens. For the future, they proposed to receive neither party unless it came peacefully in a single ship, and to treat any larger number as enemies. Having made this motion, they forced the assembly to adopt it, and at once sent envoys to Athens to justify what had been done and to dissuade the refugees there from any hostile move that might bring on a reaction.

When the embassy arrived, the Athenians arrested the envoys and all who had listened to them, as revolutionists, and lodged them in Aegina. Meanwhile a Corinthian galley arrived on the island with Lacedaemonian envoys, and the dominant Corcyraean party attacked the commons and defeated them in battle. When night came on, the commons took refuge in the Acropolis and the higher parts of the city and gathered there. They also held the Hyllaic harbor. Their adversaries occupied the market-place, where most of them lived, and the harbor next to it, which looks toward the mainland.

Nothing of importance happened the next day except skirmishes. Each party sent into the country to offer freedom to the slaves and to invite them to join it. The mass of the slaves answered the appeal of the commons, and their antagonists received reinforcements of eight hundred mercenaries from the continent.

After a day’s interval, fighting began again. The commons won, since they had the advantage in numbers and position, and the women also helped them bravely, pelting the enemy with tiles from the houses and standing up to the melee with a fortitude beyond their sex. Toward dusk the oligarchs were in full rout. They feared that the victorious commons might assault and take the arsenal and put them to the sword, so they set fire to the houses around the marketplace and to the lodging-houses, to bar the commons’ advance. They spared neither their own houses nor those of their neighbors. Much of the merchants’ stock was burned, and the city risked total destruction, if a wind had come to help the flames by blowing on them. Fighting now stopped, and both sides kept quiet and spent the night on guard. The Corinthian ship, after the victory of the commons, stole out to sea, and most of the mercenaries secretly crossed over to the continent.

The next day the Athenian general Nicostratus, son of Diitrephes, came up from Naupactus with twelve ships and five hundred Messenian heavy infantry. He at once tried to bring about a settlement. He persuaded the two parties to agree to bring ten of the ringleaders to trial (these presently fled), while the rest were to live in peace, make terms with each other, and enter into a defensive and offensive alliance with the Athenians. This arranged, he was about to sail away, when the leaders of the commons induced him to leave them five of his ships, to make their adversaries less inclined to make a move, while they would man an equal number of their own and send them with him. He had no sooner consented than they began to enroll their enemies for the ships. These men, fearing that they might be sent off to Athens, sat down as suppliants in the temple of the Dioscuri. Nicostratus tried to reassure them and to persuade them to rise, but without success. The commons then armed themselves on this pretext. They alleged that the refusal of their adversaries to sail with them proved the hollowness of their intentions, and they took their arms out of their houses. They would have killed some of those they fell in with, if Nicostratus had not prevented it. The rest of the party saw what was going on and sat down as suppliants in the temple of Hera, being not less than four hundred in number. The commons then feared that these men might take some desperate decision, and induced them to rise. They conveyed them over to the island in front of the temple, where provisions were sent across to them.

At this stage in the revolution, the fourth or fifth day after the men had been moved to the island, the Peloponnesian ships came in from Cyllene, where they had been stationed since returning from Ionia. They numbered fifty-three and were still commanded by Alcidas, though Brasidas was also on board as his adviser. They anchored at Sybota, a harbor on the mainland, and at daybreak sailed for Corcyra.

The Corcyraeans were in great confusion and alarm at the state of things in the city and at the approach of the invader. They at once began to equip sixty vessels, and sent them out against the enemy as fast as they were manned, although the Athenians recommended that the Corcyraeans let the Athenians sail out first and follow themselves afterward with all their ships together. When the Corcyraean vessels came up to the enemy in this straggling fashion, two immediately deserted. In others the crews were fighting among themselves, and there was no order in anything that was done. So the Peloponnesians, seeing their confusion, placed twenty ships against the Corcyraeans and ranged the rest against the twelve Athenian ships, among which were the two vessels Salaminia and Paralus.

The Corcyraeans attacked without judgment and in small detachments, and were already crippled by their own misconduct. The Athenians were afraid of the enemy’s numbers and of being surrounded, so they did not venture to attack the main body or even the center of the division opposed to them. They fell upon its wing and sank one vessel. After that the Peloponnesians formed in a circle, and the Athenians rowed round them and tried to throw them into disorder. The division opposed to the Corcyraeans saw this and, fearing a repetition of the disaster at Naupactus, came to support their friends. The whole fleet now bore down together upon the Athenians, who retired before it, backing water. They retired as leisurely as possible, in order to give the Corcyraeans time to escape while the enemy was kept occupied in this way. Such was the character of this sea-fight, which lasted until sunset.

The Corcyraeans now feared that the enemy would press home their victory, sail against the town and rescue the men on the island, or strike some other equally decisive blow. So they carried the men back to the temple of Hera and put a guard on the city. The Peloponnesians had won the sea-fight, yet they did not venture to attack the town. They took the thirteen Corcyraean vessels they had captured and sailed back to the continent, the point from which they had set out. The next day they again held back from the city, although the disorder and panic were at their height, and although Brasidas, it is said, pressed Alcidas, who outranked him, to attack. Instead they landed on the promontory of Leukimme and laid waste the country.

Meanwhile the commons in Corcyra were still in great fear that the fleet would attack them. To save the town, they came to a parley with the suppliants and their friends, and prevailed upon some of them to go on board the ships, of which they still manned thirty, against the expected attack. But the Peloponnesians, after ravaging the country until midday, sailed away. Toward nightfall beacon signals informed them that sixty Athenian vessels were approaching from Leucas, under the command of Eurymedon, son of Thucles. The Athenians had sent this fleet off on hearing of the revolution and of the fleet with Alcidas being about to sail for Corcyra.

The Peloponnesians therefore set off at once in haste by night for home, coasting along the shore. They hauled their ships across the Isthmus of Leucas, in order not to be seen doubling it, and so departed. The Corcyraeans learned that the Athenian fleet was approaching and the enemy had left. They brought the Messenians from outside the walls into the town and ordered the fleet they had manned to sail round into the Hyllaic harbor. While it was doing so, they killed such of their enemies as they laid hands on, and afterward, as they landed them, they dispatched those whom they had persuaded to go on board the ships. Next they went to the sanctuary of Hera and persuaded about fifty men to take their trial, and condemned them all to death. The mass of the suppliants who had refused to do so saw what was happening and killed each other there in the consecrated ground. Some hanged themselves on the trees, and others destroyed themselves as each was able. For seven days Eurymedon stayed with his sixty ships, and during that time the Corcyraeans were busy butchering those of their fellow citizens whom they regarded as their enemies. The crime charged was that of trying to put down the democracy, but some were killed also out of private hatred, and others by their debtors because of the money they owed. Death raged in every shape. As usually happens at such times, there was no length to which violence did not go. Sons were killed by their fathers, and suppliants were dragged from the altar or killed upon it. Some were even walled up in the temple of Dionysus and died there.

The revolution was so bloody in its course, and made the greater impression because it was one of the first to occur. Later, one may say, the whole Hellenic world was convulsed. In every place the popular chiefs struggled to bring in the Athenians, and the oligarchs to bring in the Lacedaemonians. In peace there would have been neither pretext nor desire to invite them. But in war either faction could always call on an alliance, to hurt its adversaries and to its own corresponding advantage, and so the revolutionary parties never lacked opportunities to bring in the foreigner. The sufferings that revolution brought on the cities were many and terrible. They have happened and always will happen, as long as human nature remains the same, though they are more severe or milder, and take different forms, according to the particular circumstances. In peace and prosperity, states and individuals hold better sentiments, because they are not suddenly confronted with imperious necessities. War, however, takes away the easy supply of daily wants, and so is a rough master, that brings most men’s characters down to the level of their fortunes. Revolution thus ran its course from city to city. The places it reached last had heard what had been done before, and went still further in refining their inventions, both in the cunning of their enterprises and in the atrocity of their reprisals. Words had to change their ordinary meaning and take the meaning now given them. Reckless audacity came to be considered the courage of a loyal ally; prudent hesitation, specious cowardice; moderation was held to be a cloak for unmanliness; the ability to see all sides of a question, an inability to act on any. Frantic violence became the mark of manliness; cautious plotting, a justifiable means of self-defense. The man who proposed extreme measures was always trusted; his opponent was suspected. To succeed in a plot was to have a shrewd head, and to detect one was to be shrewder still. But to try to make sure that you would have to do neither was to break up your party and to be afraid of your adversaries. In short, applause went equally to the man who struck first at one intending a crime and to the man who put the idea of a crime into the head of one who had never thought of it. In the end even blood became a weaker tie than party, because those bound by party were readier to dare everything without reserve. Such associations did not look to the blessings of established institutions; they were formed by ambition to overthrow them. Their members trusted each other less because of any religious sanction than because they shared in crime. The fair proposals of an adversary were met by the stronger side with jealous precautions, not with generous confidence. Revenge was also valued above self-preservation. Oaths of reconciliation were offered on either side only to meet an immediate difficulty, and held good only while no other weapon was at hand. When an opportunity came, the man who first dared to seize it, and caught his enemy off his guard, found this perfidious vengeance sweeter than an open one. Safety aside, success by treachery also won him the prize of superior intelligence. Indeed men generally find it easier to call rogues clever than simpletons honest, and are as ashamed of being the second as they are proud of being the first. The cause of all these evils was the lust for power that sprang from greed and ambition, and from these passions came the violence of parties once they were engaged in contention. The leaders in the cities each had the fairest professions: on the one side the cry of political equality for the people, on the other of a moderate aristocracy. They sought prizes for themselves in the public interests they pretended to cherish. They recoiled from no means in their struggles for ascendancy, and engaged in the direst excesses. In their acts of vengeance they went further still. They did not stop at what justice or the good of the state demanded, but made the party caprice of the moment their only standard. They were as ready to invoke the condemnation of an unjust verdict as the authority of the strong arm, to glut the animosities of the hour. Thus religion was in honor with neither party, but the use of fair phrases to arrive at guilty ends was in high reputation. Meanwhile the moderate part of the citizens perished between the two, either because they did not join in the quarrel, or because envy would not suffer them to escape.

In this way every form of iniquity took root in the Hellenic countries as a result of the troubles. The ancient simplicity, in which honor had so large a part, was laughed down and disappeared. Society became divided into camps, and in them no man trusted his fellow. There was no promise that could be depended on to end this, and no oath that could command respect. All parties rather dwelt in their calculations on the hopelessness of any permanent state of things, and were more concerned with self-defense than capable of confidence. In this contest the blunter wits were most successful. They were apprehensive of their own deficiencies and of the cleverness of their antagonists. They feared to be worsted in debate and to be surprised by the combinations of their more versatile opponents, and so they boldly turned to action at once. Their adversaries, meanwhile, arrogantly thought that they would know in time, and that there was no need to secure by action what policy could provide. They often fell victims to their want of precaution.

Meanwhile Corcyra gave the first example of most of the crimes just described. It saw the reprisals taken, when their hour came, by the governed, who had never known equitable treatment from their rulers, only insolence. It saw the iniquitous resolves of those who wished to escape their accustomed poverty and ardently coveted their neighbors’ goods. And it saw the savage and pitiless excesses into which men were carried by their ungovernable passions, men who had entered the struggle in a party spirit and not as a class. Life in the cities was now thrown into confusion. Human nature, which always rebels against the law and was now its master, gladly showed itself ungoverned in passion, above respect for justice, and the enemy of all superiority. For revenge would not have been set above religion, nor gain above justice, had it not been for the fatal power of envy. Indeed, in pursuing their revenge, men too often take it upon themselves to set the example of doing away with those general laws on which all alike can rely for salvation in adversity. They do this instead of letting them stand against the day of danger, when their aid may be needed.

The revolutionary passions had thus shown themselves for the first time in the factions of Corcyra. Then Eurymedon and the Athenian fleet sailed away. After that, some five hundred Corcyraean exiles, who had managed to escape, seized some forts on the mainland. They became masters of the Corcyraean territory across the water and used it as a base to plunder their countrymen on the island, doing so much damage that they caused a severe famine in the town. They also sent envoys to Lacedaemon and Corinth to negotiate their restoration, but had no success. Afterward they collected boats and mercenaries and crossed over to the island, about six hundred in all. They burned their boats, so as to have no hope except in becoming masters of the country, and went up to Mount Istone. There they fortified themselves, began to harass those in the city, and gained command of the country.

At the close of the same summer the Athenians sent twenty ships to Sicily, under Laches, son of Melanopus, and Charoeades, son of Euphiletus. The Syracusans and Leontines were at war there. The Syracusans had as allies all the Dorian cities except Camarina. These cities had been part of the Lacedaemonian confederacy from the start of the war, though they had taken no active part in it. The Leontines had Camarina and the Chalcidian cities. In Italy the Locrians sided with the Syracusans, and the Rhegians with their Leontine kinsmen. The allies of the Leontines now sent to Athens, appealing to their ancient alliance and to their Ionian origin, and asked the Athenians to send them a fleet, since the Syracusans were blockading them by land and sea. The Athenians sent it on the plea of their common descent, but in reality they wished to stop the export of Sicilian corn to Peloponnese and to test whether Sicily could be brought into subjection. So they established themselves at Rhegium in Italy, and from there carried on the war together with their allies.
